scenarios.title: Scenario 1 — Customer Support Resolution Agent
scenarios.brief: A meal-kit company runs a customer support agent on the Claude Agent SDK. Its MCP tools are get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human and pause_subscription. The agent may refund up to $150 per box; larger refunds go to a human.

scenarios.title: Scenario 3 — Multi-Agent Research System
scenarios.brief: A hospital's evidence team runs a research system on the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent hands work to subagents through the Task tool: literature search, trial-registry search, document analysis, citation checking, synthesis and reporting. Journals and the trial registry are reached over MCP. Summaries go to guideline committees, and every claim must cite a paper and section.

scenarios.title: Scenario 4 — Developer Productivity with Claude
scenarios.brief: A language-learning company's platform team uses Claude Code on a large Ruby on Rails app with a React front end. Engineers read and change code with the built-in tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep and Glob. MCP servers connect Claude to Linear and a staging Postgres database. Some engineers also script Claude with the Agent SDK for internal tools.

questions.question: The search subagent has two MCP tools, search_journals and search_trial_registry. Both descriptions read “Searches for studies on a drug.” Committees often ask about trials that are still running. The subagent sends these questions to search_journals, which holds only published papers, and reports that nothing was found. What is the most effective first step?

options.t: Add a routing step that sends questions about ongoing or recruiting trials to the registry tool.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. Keyword code catches the phrasings it was written for and misses the rest, and it has to be kept up as questions change.

options.t: Rewrite both descriptions: what each source holds, example queries, and when to use the other.
options.why: Best. Descriptions are what Claude reads to choose a tool. Saying what each one covers, with examples and a boundary, fixes the cause in two edits.

options.t: Merge the two tools into one search_studies tool that queries both sources at once.
options.why: Works, but more than a first step. Every question now pays for two searches, and the server and its callers have to change.

options.t: Add five example questions to the subagent's prompt, each showing which search tool to call.
options.why: Works, but misses the cause. Examples help on questions like the ones shown, add tokens to every call, and leave two identical descriptions in place.

questions.decider: Both descriptions read “Searches for studies on a drug.”
questions.explanation: Tool descriptions are the primary way Claude chooses between tools. When two tools share a vague description, the first step is to say what each one covers, with input formats, example queries and boundaries.

eli5.question: Two drawers carry the same label, “Studies”. One holds published papers; the other holds trials still running. The helper keeps opening the wrong one.
eli5.answer: Before you hire a sorter or knock the drawers together, write better labels: “Published papers: use for finished studies” and “Trials still running: use for ongoing or recruiting trials”. Claude picks tools by their descriptions the way you pick drawers by their labels. Rule: similar tools, wrong picks → fix the descriptions first.
options: A sorter at the door helps, but only for the words it was told to look for.
Correct. Clear labels on both drawers.
One big drawer works, but you search everything every time and have to rebuild the cabinet.
Showing a few examples helps, but the labels still say the same thing.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the model needs extra machinery to choose: a router, a merged tool, or examples. Claude chooses a tool mainly from its description. Two tools with the same one-line description give it nothing to choose by, so the first fix is the descriptions themselves.
deep.diagram:
question → Claude reads descriptions → picks a tool
"Searches for studies on a drug" x2 → coin toss
say what each holds + when to use the other → right pick

guide.quote: Include input formats, example queries, edge cases, boundaries.

questions.obj: 2.1 Keyword wording that pulls the wrong tool
questions.question: The system prompt says: “When a customer mentions stopping deliveries, use pause_subscription.” Company policy is that cancellations go to a person through escalate_to_human. Customers who write “stop sending boxes, I want to cancel” now get a paused plan instead. They are billed again when the pause ends. The pause_subscription description says only “Pauses deliveries.” What is the best fix?

options.t: Keep the line and add three example chats where cancelling customers are sent to a person.
options.why: Works, but only usually. The examples pull one way and the keyword line still pulls the other, so some cancellations keep getting paused.

options.t: Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks a pause when the message mentions cancelling.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. Code now guesses intent from words, and it blocks customers who say “don't cancel, just pause”.

options.t: Add a cancel_request tool that hands cancellations to staff, described for that case.
options.why: Works, but a new tool for a job escalate_to_human already does. Now three tools overlap instead of two.

options.t: Drop the keyword line, and say in each tool's description which requests it is for.
options.why: Best. The line ties a word to a tool, which is what causes the wrong pick. Clear descriptions with boundaries let Claude choose by what the customer wants.

questions.decider: When a customer mentions stopping deliveries, use pause_subscription.
questions.explanation: Keyword-sensitive system-prompt wording creates unintended tool associations. Remove the association and put each tool's purpose and boundaries in its description.

eli5.question: A sign says “Anyone who says stop, send to the pause desk.” So people who say “stop, I'm leaving” end up paused, not cancelled.
eli5.answer: Take the sign down, and label each desk by what it does: “Pause desk: a break from deliveries. Leaving for good? Go to the person at the front.” Rule: a prompt line that ties a word to a tool causes misrouting → remove it and put the boundary in the tool descriptions.
options: Showing people the right desk helps, but the sign still points the wrong way.
A guard who stops anyone saying “cancel” also stops people who said “don't cancel”.
A new desk for leavers works, but the front desk already does that job.
Correct. Remove the misleading sign and label the desks.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a misrouting needs new code or a new tool. Here the system prompt itself causes it: a keyword rule sends any mention of stopping to one tool. Remove the cause, and give each tool a description that says what it is for and what it is not for.
deep.diagram:
"stop ... cancel" → prompt rule: stop = pause → paused
rule gone + clear descriptions → escalate_to_human

deep.rule: A prompt line ties a word to a tool? Remove it, and put the boundary in the tool descriptions.

guide.obj: 2.1 Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries
guide.quote: Ambiguous/overlapping descriptions cause misrouting; keyword-sensitive system-prompt wording creates unintended tool associations.

questions.obj: 2.3 Too many tools for one agent
questions.question: An Agent SDK script triages new bug reports in Linear. It was given every tool from both MCP servers, 18 in all, plus the built-in tools. Its job needs about five of them. It often calls update_issue when it should call move_issue. Sometimes it queries staging when no data is involved. Every tool already has a detailed description. What is the best fix?

options.t: Rewrite all the tool descriptions with sharper boundaries between issue and database tools.
options.why: Works, but misses the cause. The descriptions are already detailed; the number of tools is what lowers the choice quality.

options.t: Add a classifier that reads each bug report and picks which tools to offer for it.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. The script does one job, so its tool set can be fixed once instead of chosen per report.

options.t: Give the triage script only the tools its job needs and leave the rest out.
options.why: Best. Fewer tools make the choice more reliable, and a triage script has no reason to reach the database.

options.t: Merge update_issue and move_issue into one change_issue tool with a mode field.
options.why: Works, but fixes one pair. The choice moves into a parameter, and the database calls still happen.

questions.decider: It was given every tool from both MCP servers, 18 in all, plus the built-in tools.
questions.explanation: Giving an agent many tools degrades selection reliability, and tools outside its role get misused. Scope each agent to the tools its job needs.

eli5.question: A helper sorting mail has been handed every tool in the building, and keeps grabbing the wrong one.
eli5.answer: Better labels on 18 tools still leave 18 tools to pick from. Give the mail sorter the five things a mail sorter needs. Rule: wrong picks among many tools, with good descriptions already → cut the agent's tool set to its job.
options: Clearer labels help, but the labels are already good and the pile is still too big.
A helper who hands out tools for each letter works, but the job never changes.
Correct. Give the sorter only the tools for sorting.
Gluing two tools together fixes one mix-up, not the pile.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think every wrong pick is a description problem. Descriptions come first when they are vague. Here they are already detailed, and the agent holds far more tools than its job needs. Too many tools degrade the choice, and tools outside the role get misused.
deep.diagram:
18 tools + built-ins → triage script → wrong picks
5 triage tools → triage script → right picks

evidence.means: The decider: the tool count is the cause.

evidence.means: A tool outside its job gets misused. Merging two issue tools ([[3]]) leaves this in place.

deep.rule: Good descriptions and still wrong picks among many tools? Give the agent only the tools its job needs.
